text:
Minecraft needs biome overhauls

I think for future Minecraft Game Drops, Mojang should take a break from adding new biomes and instead focus on improving the ones that already exist.

What if each Game Drop was dedicated to fully updating one type of biome?
For example, the next winter update could overhaul all snowy and cold biomes at once. That would include better atmosphere, new mobs that actually fit the environment, and gameplay mechanics that make those biomes more interesting and worth exploring.

Right now, a lot of biomes feel kind of empty or outdated compared to newer content. This would be a great opportunity to bring them up to the same level.
It would also be the perfect time to finally update the losing biomes from past biome votes like the savanna, desert, and badlands. they really need attention at this point. Maybe even add new structures specific to each biome to make exploration more rewarding.
Also, Minecraft has mentioned that they want to improve the “adventure” side of the game, which basically means exploration. Focusing on biome overhauls would fit perfectly with that goal, since it would make exploring the world feel much more meaningful and varied.

Overall, I feel like focusing on depth instead of constantly adding new biomes would make the game feel much more alive and balanced.

text:
Phantoms are just awful

I recently started playing Minecraft for the first time in almost 8 years. I noticed that these mobs shape player behavior negatively. First, they discourage exploration because it forces players to either be pestered endlessly or go to bed (i.e. change spawn point, waste time in an unfun loop). It bothers builders endlessly by forcing them off their builds or being threatened with being knocked off. The combat is not fun or challenging, the reward is laughable.
The theme of the mob doesn't even fit the overworld, it looks like they were designed for a unique biome but were just slapped onto a "spawn on top of player" rule.
The following are the most common responses:

"I've never had any problems." | Congratulations, you can think about yourself! Pat yourself on the back.

"Just turn it off using game rules or when creating the world" | You do realize that this is admittance of bad mob design? Instead of fixing the mob they just tacked on an extra checkbox to "fix" their poor execution of a mob.
"Just go to bed, it takes 2 seconds" | These people seem to think that the quick and easy (and unrewarding) nature of defeating this mob absolves its inadequacies, it makes them WORSE. All that hassle for a boring loop. Being taken off of your mega projects to tap a bed and then climb all the way back up to not be pestered relentlessly is NOT FUN. Debating exploring your world because of the 3 day limit or be forced to change your spawn point to thousands of blocks away from your base is NOT FUN.
"It was a mob vote, the community wanted this" | LOL. This would be somewhat true if Mojang had some actual transparency at showing what the mobs would actually be like instead of vague descriptions. Had the community known that THIS is what they would end up with for nearly a decade I'm certain they would have chosen another mob. Why on Earth did they wait to announce the Aquatic update until AFTER the mob vote?
"Its already been X years, Mojang will never change it now." | Part of the problem, its called pride. This isn't the strong argument you guys seem to think it is.

text:
Who else never uses the elytra?

First of all, I fully respect and appreciate that most players love the elytra, so it obviously shouldn’t be removed from the game.

But I’ve been playing since 2012, and I’ve never touched the elytra.

I just know that it would instantly make my gameplay experience worse.
First of all, it largely takes the “survival” out of survival Minecraft, in my opinion. Dangerous terrain? Just fly over it. Surrounded by mobs? Just fly away. Fall from a cliff? No problem—you can fly. And when you then add automatic farms and shulker boxes, aren’t you just playing Creative with extra steps?
The biggest issue for me, however, is that it takes all the intrinsic motivation out of building infrastructure.
I love building infrastructure. I don’t just want to build pretty things; I want to build functional things that expand my horizons: railroads, bridges, tunnels, horse infrastructure, harbors, nether hubs, ender pearl cannons.
The elytra negates the functionality of pretty much all of that.
I know some will say it’s an “endgame item.” But my games don’t end after beating the dragon. Why should my “end-game” be less fun than early/mid game. I always have lots more to do, including things that are much more advanced than beating the Ender Dragon. Are those things easier with an elytra? Yes. They would also be easier in Creative mode, but they would be a hell of a lot less fun to accomplish, in my opinion.
But I’m clearly in the minority on this. I’m just interested to hear from others like me, and also to hear if anyone has arguments for why I should give the elytra a chance.

text:
Mending, the "two-week Minecraft phase", and what progression should mean

Open discussion, relating some different ideas I've seen floating around.

  1. Mending is absolutely imperative for anything late-game and the game would be a tedious slog without it or if it was harder to get

  2. Minecraft is more fun early game / there is a lack of late-game content / "the two-week Minecraft phase"

Hopefully you can see how these are in conflict with each other, at least a bit.
"Why does Mending matter if you only like the early game?"

"If you like the danger and grind of the early game, why do you also like an enchantment that in some ways removes that?"

---

Jeb recently made a somewhat controversial comment about items and Mending: https://bsky.app/profile/jebox.bsky.social/post/3me4d6q52sk2h

> The purpose of the [anvil level] cap is that all items are intended to be impermanent. Mending is a different issue.
This sparked some debate around the original design of Minecraft vs. how most people prefer to play these days, even arguably how the game has actually become more recently with the additions of nonrenewable/ultra-rare items like the Elytra, Trident, Mace, etc.

One user pointed this out and Jeb conceded that point: https://bsky.app/profile/jebox.bsky.social/post/3meh2f34yck2h
> I’m not opposed to tools being impermanent by nature, especially since it gives more incentive to mine, but I’m surprised that it’s a part of MC’s philosophy since armor trims felt like something of an anthesis to the idea to me. Were armor trims designed with mending in mind or moreso extra mining?

> (Jeb) Yeah, you bring up a good point
Regardless of the original intent of Minecraft, many item additions in recent years are unavoidably counter to that. How are both of these philosophies present in the game? Wouldn't this create a fractured experience?

In some ways yes (anvil level cap, losing items on death feels wrong late-game, etc), but I think in other ways the community actually generally likes both, and we think of it as "early-game grind" vs "late-game min-maxing" and call it... "progression"!
Honestly I think this is a bit of a new idea in the gaming world and has become more mainstream with games like Terraria, Stardew Valley, etc. that have very distinct and uniquely fun early-game, mid-game, and late-game content. Since Minecraft is also a sandbox game, I think community sentiment has pushed Mojang to make their game more like that over the years.
This is is a bit different from the original experience of the game, so I think it makes sense it's begun to cause some conflict with existing systems in the game.
These days, we are expecting a sense of progression. Early game and late game should be distinct from one another but have unique challenges and systems. Historically, Minecraft early game is great and has always been great, but late game is lacking, even though Mojang has added tons to it in recent years.
Circling back to Mending, you could argue it "removes" some of the grind aspect, but in reality it's a natural response to how difficult and satisfying some late-game items are to get. The early-game grind of crafting new pickaxes IS fun when they're just iron or even diamond, but once you get your fully enchanted Netherite, you want that to be a one-and-done deal. I'd argue this distinction didn't used to exist in the game, and didn't when the existing enchanting and anvil systems were set up.
Finally, to answer the conflict in the statements at the beginning of this post, it's probably this:

Early game IS more fun... AND late game would be even worse without Mending, precisely because of how many difficult late-game items have been added (for better or for worse).

It's almost like Mojang "opened that can of worms themselves" and now has to deal with two different game stages and how they interact, and sometimes conflict with each other:

  1. Early game (what Minecraft has always been)
  2. Late game (what Minecraft has been becoming)

I just think it's good to point out that these are "growing pains" with a game that's seen a lot of cool evolution without sacrificing much of the original experience.
Some people haven't really broken into late-game so don't understand the reliance on Mending, or wouldn't care if it was removed. Others have different ideas about how early game and late game are supposed to interact entirely, which has all sorts of differences in how Mending should be treated.
The whole "Mending debacle" is such a hot topic because it goes straight to the game's roots and how it's been changing over the years. I'm very curious what they're going to do with it long-term, and what that means for the game's new philosophy going forward. Even though discussions can get heated I always find the different ideas very interesting!

---
Final thought: with a game as infinite as Minecraft, you cannot "beat" it. Every time you put it down, it will inevitably end with "boredom" rather than "I did it". I think this leaves a weird taste in your mouth with it looking back, even if you had an amazing time with it for months, way longer than almost any other game.
Sometimes I wonder if this is actually the main contributor to the "Minecraft isn't fun anymore" or "Minecraft's fundamental problem" takes, just people remembering how it ended rather than how it actually was.

text:
The Inventory Problem™️

Since this is a hot topic among the community and keeps coming up in discussion regarding new updates, I wanted to drop in my two cents since these points usually get buried under piles of complaints and plain counterpoints that complaints are entitled.
# The core issue

The raw number of different items and blocks has expanded significantly and will keep doing so, no way around it. While back in the day, an inventory of 36 slots was enough to carry just about everything you'd ever need realistically, this has changed.
Undeniably, the amount of items multiplied immensely since these days, build styles have emerged that were not a thing back then, build palettes have become more complex. Mobs drop more stuff, not on a per-mob basis but the overall variety of drops. Environments have more ambient plants and various doodads. Redstone requires more and more specialized components.

Of course this is a good thing. It's a natural consequence of the game being alive and well.
It does mean however that things that used to be quick and easy to do have become more cumbersome. And solving this will always have to be compatible with both Java and Bedrock, all supported deviced and all the supported input methods from touch through gamepad to mouse/keyboard and beyond.
# The suggested change

> Just increase the inventory, that'd fix everything

Lots of people usually request this not seeing that, no, it wouldn't fix everything. And Mojang know this.

Increasing the inventory has a couple of issues that people like to overlook. It's fighting inflating numbers with inflating other numbers.
We already established that the raw number of items in this game will continue to grow. This is inevitable. This means if increasing the inventory is the fix, the player's inventory will become unwieldy. People will complain that they can't find in their inventories what they need to access. Depending on the client they might need to scroll. The next request will be tabbed inventory, a bigger hotbar, more hotbars, bigger stack sizes, ...
Players will have to juggle more and more types of tools, weapons, blocks, decoration, redstone components, whatever depending on what they're doing at the moment. Controlling a cursor with a gamepad across a huge grid of items could become troublesome, especially if it has to happen quickly.
# Mojang's approach

Mojang is already tackling this problem in very smart ways and people often dismiss these approaches, thinking each one of them is supposed to solve "the" inventory problem while each solves "a" inventory issue and collectively they will solve it sustainably.

A quick recap on what we have right now:

  * 2013: Donkeys and Mules have the ability to carry chests, effectively increasing the player's inventory on land by 15 slots.
  * 2016: Shulker Boxes allow the player to carry chests with their whole inventory, 27 additional slots in a single slot. Llamas also offer the ability to carry chests, but in contrast to donkeys and mules, they have the caravan mechanic which means up to nine llamas in sum can increase a player's inventory on land by 135 slots.
  * 2019: The barrel is a slightly cheaper storage option, the stonecutter reduces the number of items you usually need to transport while building. Campfires allow cooking food without using the inventory.

  * 2022: Chest Boats are added, increasing the inventory on water by 27 slots. Allays offer a new option for handling items in specific situations without needing to spend time in the inventory. While this was a community vote, the choice to offer the allay was very much concious on Mojang's side.
  * 2023: The decorated pot and the chiseled bookshelf also reduce the amount the player actually spends in their inventory when using certain items.

  * 2024: The crafter again reduces the amount the player actually is required to handle stuff in their inventory manually. Bundles allow stacking multiple, up to 64, different items in a single slot.
  * 2025: Leads allow transport of multiple chest mobs and chest boats at the same time, immensely increasing the player's effective inventory. Copper Golems were conciously picked up from a past vote by Mojang, and explicitly changed from their former mechanic to a new behaviour which, again, offers to reduce the time a player is required to spend in their inventory.
Shelves allow swapping up to 9 inventory slots at once without even opening the inventory, streamlining the handling of items and tools immensely.
# Observations

Especially in the more recent years, it's incredibly obvious that Mojang know perfectly well that inventory and item handling are a very complex problem that need a series of parallel approaches to solve them reliably for good.

They apparently try to follow multiple philosophies at the same time:

  * In general reduce the time the player needs to spend in the inventory at all

  * Make handling items in specific situations more streamlined
  * Increase the inventory in specific situations with trade-offs
And this is a way smarter approach than just increasing the inventory flat out. If done well, reducing the time in the inventory means players are less likely to run into situations where the inventory becomes a problem at all. Streamlining handling items means situations where the inventory has become a problem are quicker and easier to deal with.
Increasing the inventory with trade-offs then allows for niche situations to offer a bonus while asking the player to actually engage with the game's mechanics.
# The future

From these observations we can make a few fair estimations as to where we're headed.

  * Increased inventory while travelling across lava. I think Striders carrying chests is too obvious, but some kind of other lavaborne, swimming mob that can carry a few chests while being slower than the Strider seems likely to me.
  * A more streamlined way to specifically handle only tools and weapons inside the inventory. Some kind of toolbelt that allows to stack multiple tools into one slot and allows switching between them without needing to open the inventory.

  * Switching of the currently equipped armor quickly. This might be done as an update to the armor stand or as a new block that works like the powered shelf and allows for switching the currently equipped whole armor set with the stored one.
  * A palette item storing a variety of dyes for using multiple dyes without handling them in the inventory manually.
  * More direct interactions with blocks for specialized storage. I could see specialized record racks for storing stacks of record discs, some kind of pantry for holding food items, storing an arbitrary amount of one color dye in a paint bucket block, potion racks, specialized storage for ores, ingots, seeds, among others. These will most likely be handling a single type of item with huge variations or a lot of different items that all work the same way.
  * A way to simply replace a block or transform it in its location. Examples would be a smelting spell that transforms a block into its furnace output at a cost or cuts blank stone into bricks or logs into planks. Maybe something that allows the transformation of any already placed wood product into a different wood.
In my opinion, we are actually likely to see a couple of these across the next couple of years. If a simple increased inventory comes at all, it will probably come at a cost. A backpack that gives a single extra row of 9 slots at the cost of not being able to wear armor is a common suggestion that seems realistic to me. But I don't think this will actually be that necessary long term, if the already established philosophies are followed and implemented to their full potential.
Solving the situations where the inventory frustration actually comes up is way more useful than delaying the problem a couple updates into the future.

text:
Community is wrong about latest updates.

Let's talk about Minecraft updates. For quite a while now, it’s become trendy to complain about every single update, claiming that "this isn't it" and that "the old days were better." This is pretty typical for any gaming community, so it's no surprise. These people love to say that Notch should never have sold the game, while completely forgetting things like the Horse Update (1.6.1)—which added horses, leads, hay bales, donkeys, and other minor tweaks.
That update wasn't bad at all, but it was very much in the spirit of the "minor" updates Mojang has been releasing lately. However, I think these smaller updates are actually the right approach. Imagine you're looking for a new biome with fresh mobs and mechanics. Every new mob has polished animations (like the Sniffer or the Warden), but to get there, you have to fly over empty areas that haven't been touched since 2012. Is THAT actually fun for anyone? Now, let’s look at recent and semi-recent updates.
They added the Camel, which livened up the desert and allows for two riders. They revamped the oceans with dolphins, new structures, and dangerous Drowned with tridents. They added new skeleton variants (Bogged in swamps, Strays in snowy biomes) and introduced different wolf breeds depending on the biome. All these updates breathe life into old biomes that had become stale and boring due to a lack of changes.
I’m also hoping they’ll finally fully implement the Illusioner pillager soon, since he’s basically ready anyway. These minor updates Mojang has been putting out lately aren’t bad at all, and I’m all for them continuing this path. If you’re just mindlessly whining about updates—especially if you’re just parroting some YouTuber’s "opinion"—it’s worth stopping to think and looking at the actual pros of these changes. I should also say a few words about the community.
Some people—actually, a fairly large portion of players—stick to old versions instead of moving to the new ones. The only valid reason to do this is performance, as newer versions are more demanding on your hardware. New versions of Minecraft are essentially the same "old" Minecraft, just with a ton of cool new features. Nothing has objectively gotten worse from update to update; it has only improved.
If you play old versions and aren't afraid to admit it’s just for nostalgia or because your PC can’t handle the new stuff, then I have no issues with you. But when you claim the game has "mysteriously" become worse and that people should stay on old versions, you’re just lying to yourself, and you’re dead wrong.
These minor updates Mojang has been putting out lately aren’t bad at all, and I’m all for them continuing this path. If you’re just mindlessly whining about updates—especially if you’re just parroting some YouTuber’s "opinion"—it’s worth stopping to think and looking at the actual pros of these changes.

text:
Minecraft has pumpkins, bowls, and 15 years of missed opportunity

To whom it may concern,

I write this as a plea of desperation, mere weeks before my 25th birthday.

The humble pumpkin was added to Minecraft in Java Edition Alpha v1.2.0 in 2010, and my nine-year-old self was delighted. As the years passed, more craftable items emerged from our orange friend. And yet, even then, I began to feel the cold fingers of existential dread tugging at my child-sized Creeper attire.
For although we were able to create soups and stews of many kinds, the transcendental ecstasy of pumpkin soup remained forever barred from my grasp.

For years, my tiny child mind, unburdened by the knowledge of dev teams, update cycles, and feature prioritisation, persevered. I tried a pumpkin and a bowl. I tried milk, pumpkin, and a bowl. I even turned to pumpkin seeds in a futile attempt to craft this long-denied delicacy.

But no.
Although the pumpkin was right there, the opportunity ripe, and my heart hopeful, pumpkin soup remained uncraftable.

Now I build temples and empires. I have seen civilisations rise and fall. I have watched dimensions appear out of thin air. I have sat in hobbit holes, witch’s hovels, and pristine cherry blossom cottages. Yet through it all, Steve has never once raised to his lips the wholesome, life-altering comfort of pumpkin soup.
And so I carry an emptiness. A quiet ache. The knowledge that my Minecraft experience has never reached its full potential for true, wholesome coziness.

Minecraft Dev Team, if you exist, somewhere in your sacred order of developers: I have lived in a pumpkin-soupless purgatory for over fifteen years.

As my brain reaches full maturation at the age of 25, I ask now, with the faint light of hope flickering within me:

Please.

Add pumpkin soup to Minecraft.

text:
Should Minecraft be less... Eurocentric?

I wish Minecraft focused more on making the game better at representing all people, cultures, and places. Often, I will want to build things like a Middle Eastern town or a Polynesian village and come to the sad conclusion that I am trying to build non-European things with a blocky European farm/fantasy sandbox. Sure there have been some improvements in this regard but at this rate, I'll be able to access my retirement account before I see a palm tree in the game.
I believe if Minecraft focused a small amount on additions and improvements regarding food and ambiance (biomes and mobs), then it will finally start feeling like a complete world sandbox game. Also, more diversity in art and items for interiors could be really nice.
First, with food. Why is wheat the only grain? Why no rice, corn, coconuts, grapes, dates, or tropical fruits? Adding a few foods that are bedrock to different cultures would considerably help expand how this game feels.
Do you want to live like a Pacific Islander cultivating coconuts, raising pigs, and growing taro, then sail off into the sunset? Now you can! Do you want to role play as a Chinese peasant, tending rice paddies on suspiciously flat and fertile soil around a river that totally wont flood and carry away your home? I sure do!
Second, biomes. Harder lift, but we all know there are biomes that need more love than others. Meadows? Splendid. Taiga, especially old growth, is majestic and tranquil. The biomes that dominate Europe such as forests, taiga, mountains, plains, and meadows seem more complete and thoughtfully improved. Jungles, deserts, and badlands among others desperately need some life breathed into them, whether in more interesting stuff or plants, or literally with more life as in mobs.
Lastly, and perhaps most controversially, theres mobs and our interactions with them. Mojang has taken quite a thoughtful approach to adding new mobs, often disincentivizing players from killing them and not adding mobs they think could be harmful. But I believe their methods in doing so have been too severe and have been a hinderance to making other cultures come to life in Minecraft.
You can be a cow farmer in the Swiss Alps living off of your dairy and beef, but you can't live like a nomadic Bedouin or Mongolian goat herder, subsisting off of your flock (no meat!). By restricting all meat and most basic drop sources to typical European farm animals, it severely limits play styles for other cultures.
Adding temperature variability for cows, pigs and chickens was a great step in the right direction, but theres much more to do! Interacting with animals, including harvesting from them, is so important to so many cultures. Mojang is too concerned with unethical animal interaction and endangered species representation and it is holding Minecraft back. It forces the same playthroughs (steakmaxxing) and nerfs the wildlife ambiance.
And before you say "just add mods", I believe these things are the basics that a good sandbox game like Minecraft should have, and I think these considerations would greatly improve the base game in its sandbox capacity.
So please Minecraft, grow beyond the Eurocentric sandbox you are and become the world sandbox game you were destined to be! I dream that one day I will be able to ride horses hunting bison on the plains, shear llamas or subsist entirely on goats high in the mountains, and grow rice among coconut trees on the edge of a jungle, trying to keep out elephants from trampling my paddies. One day...

text:
Diamonds aren't rare, and you don't need to hoard them like a dragon with its gold

People have talked about jukebox being expensive for a long time, and I saw this mentioned many times since the last snapshot released, so I just wanted to explain why from my point of view it's simply not true.
First of all, let's establish the use cases diamonds actually have in Minecraft:

  * Tools

  * Weapons

  * Armor

  * Templates duplication

  * Enchanting table crafting

  * Jukeboxes
With Mending being a thing, once you craft your tools, weapons and armor, you almost never need to replace them, and if you do - you can buy new tools, weapons and armor from vilalgers and disenchant it to put the enchantments you need on them, so you don't actually need diamonds for that, it's a one time investment at most.

So the player doesn't need that many diamonds before they become mostly irrelevant to them as a resource in the game.

But how do you actually find diamonds, and is it hard to do?
Simple and short answer is that finding diamonds isn't hard at all.
Long answer is, finding diamonds is easy, because there's a lot of ways to do that. The most obvious is going to a cave and just looking around, you'll find tons of them very reliably, and if you have Fortune on your pickaxe, as one should, you'll be literally drowning in them. Simply find an opening to a big cave on the surface, go down, and there's so many of them, you'll be catching yourself missing multiple veins of diamonds, because you notice a different vein and went to it.
But what's there other than caves? Well, there's lots and lots of structures. You can find diamonds in shipwrecks, and shipwrecks have maps that lead you to buried chests, that also have diamonds in them. There's also diamonds in villages, abandoned mineshafts, desert temples, trial chambers, stronghold, and now also abandoned camps.

And it doesn't stop with the overworld, there's diamonds in bastions, nether fortresses, and end cities. Especially end cities, there's loads of them in the end cities.
All you have to do is explore the world.

Conclusion

I have no issues with the jukebox using a single diamond in its crafting recipe, because I don't need these diamonds anyway, and I always find more and more of them. And if you'd ever leave your base? So would you.
Mojang is very clearly aiming to add more things for players to explore, but I notice that a lot of players just stick to sitting at their base forever, never leaving to explore the world, which in some cases leads to players having a very hard time gathering any resources, not just diamonds, hence everything seems "too expensive".
Maybe I'm wrong, because I never needed and never intend to need 10000 jukeboxes for any build, I see it as more of a complementary decorative block, maybe something subtle to use for a wall, but not something I would ever need hundreds and thousands of, hence why the crafting recipe doesn't bother me. I could craft a few stacks and have enough for decorations in my builds for months.

text:
Tridents Need A Rehaul.

I'm gonna get on here to critique the trident real quick.
Let's start with the whole impaling mess. So, in Java, impaling only affects specific tagged "aquatic" mobs. This includes a bunch of fodder, passive mobs like squid, fish, dolphins, all that jazz. However, THE underwater enemy, drowned, is utterly unaffected by it, because it's classified as "undead". Why is this enchantment so much better on bedrock? If the mob is in water or rain, you get the damage buff, period. It's intuitive and actually useful.
Monuments are essentially the only place where it's relevant, as guardians are the only aquatic hostile mob. Loyalty and riptide are literally the only good enchantments, everything else is super niche.
Oh, I can't critique the trident without discussing the acquisition. This is the laziest part honestly. It's supposed to be a "special weapon", while not being tied to any structure, not engaging in any way to acquire, it's just a monotonous RNG slot machine that drops from a common mob like most other weapons. Same 8.5% chance—like only 6.25% of drowned spawn with a trident to drop one at all. For the record, why on bedrock, 15% of drowns spawn with a trident, and they have a 25% chance of dropping it.
WHY?
After all that, they typically drop at low durability too, like 40% at best, but it can get real low, like in the single digits. Since they’re not tied to a crafting recipe or a specific material, guess what you need to repair a trident… another trident. Yea, so mending is non-negotiable.
It's especially glaring when you look at the spears and their unique animations and distinctive mechanics, despite literally being as cheap and easy to make as a shovel, meanwhile you have the trident over here stuck being a clunky, niche gimmick that's hardly even worth an inventory slot. I understand it's not a modern weapon, but still, it feels half finished. It literally bleeds potential. Like, you can imagine how awesome it could've been, but the execution is so lazy in virtually every department.
It feels clunky to use as a melee weapon because it uses same canned swing animation as any other item, and again, look at the spear, hell the mace too, then back at the trident. See what I mean? You can't unsee it.
It definitely didn't get the respect it should've on bedrock either, but it's still better than the java shitshow. Don’t just buff it, rehaul it. Give it new mechanics, animations, and a powerful identity.

text:
What are genuine arguments against an item stack increase?

According to the wiki, there are 1,643 items in the game as of 1.20 (the number is gonna be even higher after this next content drop).

lets compare this to terraria
In terraria, 1.2 increased the item stack limit from 250 to 999. Can't get a solid number, but there were about 1,800 items in terraria in 1.2. Terraria also increased the chest storage size from 30-40 in 1.2, had dedicated ammo and trash slots in 1.0.6, and quick stack, sorting, and deposit all buttons in 1.3.
Minecraft has almost the same amount of items as there were in terraria 1.2, but there has not been an item stack increase in the entire lifespan of the game, or even any kind of inventory management other than bundles and shulker boxes (shulker's are endgame content).
you can make the argument that they are different games with different needs, but if anything that points to Minecraft needing an item increase more than terraria does. Minecraft, as a 3d game, needs far more building materials than terraria. Minecraft has a smaller base inventory size than terraria (37 vs 50, not including dedicated ammo, money, and multiple armor and accessory slots), and has far fewer options for remote storage.
To have 250 items in Minecraft, you need to dedicate 4 inventory slots, which is 10% of your inventory. Pre 1.2 terraria, 250 items took up 2% of your inventory.
So what do you guys think? I feel like we're getting to the point where stack increases, and other inventory management, are becoming necessary. I dont wanna hear any BS about how 64 is an iconic number, that's just using nostalgia as an excuse to not move forward with the game. nothing will stop you from keeping your own stacks at 64 if you like the number

text:
The Minecraft Devs are NOT lazy but it’s perfectly reasonable to expect more new content than drops have added

This is gonna be a long one.

TLDR- Minecraft content has been great but each drop feels like it is missing a few core features that would add excitement and significant content. The developers are not lazy, they are simply understaffed for Minecraft being one of the most popular games in the world.
To start, I do not believe the devs are lazy in the slightest. The amount of effort it takes to create updates for a variety of platforms that all have to have nearly identical content despite using different engines, systems, etc is enormous. Their work is staggering and their ability to keep Minecraft relevant for so long after its release is genuinely incredible. This post is not at all meant to hate on the developers.
That being said, it is perfectly reasonable to expect more content than what is being offered from Minecraft. Minecraft is one of the most popular games ever made. It spawned a plethora of art, games, books, videos, creativity and much much more. Its influence on Western culture cannot be understated and its reach goes far beyond the gaming sphere. Minecraft makes billions of dollars each year when you add up merchandising sales, game add ons, and more.
Despite these things, the content added to Minecraft has felt like less and less, especially since the drop system was added, and expecting slightly more content is a valid sentiment.
I do not hate the drop system, nor do I love it. I believe it has its pros and cons like all things, but one of the worst cons is that updates feel much less special and eventful than they used to. Obviously the drops were always going to have less content than major updates, but there is a more significant difference than many of us realized there would be. Although adding up all the content from multiple drops may stack up to the same size as an update, it certainly doesn’t feel that way.
While drops allow you to focus on specific features, this can leave may players on the outs; if the drop theme or features don’t interest you or don’t particularly cater to your play-style, you are out of luck for the foreseeable future. In contrast, updates normally were more well rounded with content for many different play-styles. To conclude, I do not think drops are inherently negative, but I believe each one would have felt immensely better with only one or two more significant features.
Rather than have one big focus (happy ghast, baby mobs, mounts), drops should aim to have two to three features that will significantly impact gameplay and can bring the hype back to Minecraft updates. Some drops are better than others, but they could all use just a pinch more to make them feel memorable and worthwhile.
Ultimately, I believe that Minecraft makes more than enough money to expand their developer team. I am not talking about doubling their staff or anything, but having 10-20 more people working on new content for the base game would add so much to the player experience and would allow them to spread their ideas and experiences out amongst a larger team.
Imagine if Pale Gardens came with a unique structure like a mansion or a graveyard, imagine if the spring drop included updated ambiance to snow and the Savannah biomes. These are just some ideas that demonstrate why I find the drop system to be decent, but not great. Each drop ALWAYS feels like it could have benefitted from just a tad more developer time to truly flesh out the content.
I find it ridiculous that a company with as much money as Microsoft does not have the funds to give us more than a few small features and one major feature every few months. I think the devs are doing a wonderful job, but a few more could foster more meaningful content for a diverse audience of players.
I want to address some of the responses I foresee getting regarding these ideas. Firstly, the main response I see in opposition to asking for more content is “you are still receiving content 15 years later for a game that you paid $20 for.” While initially this does seem rational, this does not at all account for the marketability of Minecraft. Realms and the Marketplace are two massive micro transactions that many Minecraft players have purchased at least once if not thousands of times.
This along with merchandise sales, the in person experiences, the upcoming theme park, spinoff games, A Minecraft Movie, and more all have filled the pockets of Microsoft to the brim, yet the updates still don’t feel fully fleshed out. Despite some players only paying once, a large amount of Minecraft players have poured much more money into the game in a variety of ways. This money should be funneled back into the development of the game, more so than it already is.
Vanilla minecraft has to keep the hype rolling and the drop system seems to lose more and more hype the longer it goes on.
Now obviously this post was at least partially inspired by today’s Minecraft Live and I want to also address many of the comments I’ve seen regarding it. First, I think the content they revealed looks great. I’m super excited for sulfur and the Sulfur Cube looks like one of the most unique ideas we’ve had in a while. I’ve seen a few people critique this drop as being low on content and many in the comments telling them to wait for future snapshots as they do not show everything at Minecraft Live.
While this is true, the content added that is not shown off at Minecraft Live has NEVER been significant. We may get a new mob variant or more variants of new blocks. We may even get a recipe change or two, but none of this is particularly significant especially compared to what updates used to bring. For example, imagine if sulfur could be a new system that interacts with smelting, or if it was used to create new variants of TNT.
Just like the previous drops, this is shaping up to be a good drop that feels undeveloped and could have used more time to be fully fleshed out.
Another argument I hear a lot is “if you want more content why don’t you just go play marketplace, mods, etc. I’ve always disliked this argument because player-created content should never be expected in place of actual content for the mainline game. While I enjoy the experiences that these side modes can give, vanilla Minecraft is the core of the game and should be treated as such.
Additions to vanilla are always the most anticipated features in the community because that is quite literally the whole game. Any additional features are just that - additional, and they cannot replace core game content.
Lastly, the Tiny Takeover drop is the ultimatum of what I’ve been discussing. This drop is the first one in my eyes to truly drop the ball in terms of the scope and scale of the content. I like what they added, but having an entire drop dedicated to just this feels extremely lackluster and disappointing. I understand that this drop is largely focused on under the hood changes, but that doesn’t change the fact that the amount content we are getting is so so small.
This again shows that Minecraft needs more developers. That way they can split up game content and internal changes even more to create a more efficient and effective process. As is, Tiny Takeover has given me no motivation to check it out and the community hype is at an all time low.
In conclusion, I believe that Minecraft should expand their development team so that each drop can feel more focused and fleshed out. Minecraft makes more than enough money to add on a few team members that can help to make drops feel significant and exciting again. The developers are not lazy or out of touch, they just do not currently have the manpower to reach the needs of a game on the scale of Minecraft.
If you made it this far, thank you for reading. I think the talks around the most recent drops and Minecraft as a whole has lacked a lot of nuance, so I hope the comments can engage in good discussion that focuses on the central issues instead of argument for the sake of it. Let me know what you think about anything I mentioned here.
label: proposal

text:
Why the Sift Update MIGHT introduce magic/sorcery into Minecraft.

This isn't speculation or a theory as much as it's a desire I believe is most possible now than it ever was. Here are my points :

IN MINECRAFT LORE, SOULS = MAGIC
Souls have been inherently linked to magic since before Dungeons which has only cemented it. Netherwart grows only on Soulsand, creating potions which when used to kill create the deathtag 'Killed by Magic'. Soul speed enchantments cause literal souls to rise from the sand.
'Souls' and 'experience' seem to be somewhat interchangeable or exchangeable. You obtain experience through killing things, or actions which build the amount of experience you have. And, with your death, you releases this experience. It fuels and spreads Sculk (which finds it's origin in the Sift). It's the required fuel for enchantments of any kind.
Within Minecraft Dungeons, having any Soul Item gives you a Soul Meter (which functions similarly to an experience meter). You gain more by killing Mobs. This fuel is used for many magical items, including the Corrupted Beacon, Lightning Scepter, etc. and Soul Related Wearable Gear usually has a wizard/sorcery theme.
In Minecraft dungeons 2, the Evoker, Illusionist and Enchanter (all mage archetypes) are utilising the Soul Block as the source of their power, and creating the portals to the Sift in the first place.

My point here is that within Minecraft 'lore', Souls and Magic are always connected. Everything remotely magical in some way connects to souls.

THE SIFT & SOULS

Moreover, the Sift is HEAVILY connected to the theme of Souls. I don't need to explain this very much as I believe that's quite obvious.
The Soul Block, the object which is central to Dungeons 2 as the power source of the High Councils Magic is from the Sift. The Sculk, a soul fueled mass is from the Sift. The liquid seen in the Sift is the damaging Ichor, described as literal concentrated Souls.

Minecraft seems to be REALLY pushing this Soul theme, huh?

HOW MAGIC MIGHT APPEAR
This doesn't mean I expect to see magic, nor does it give me an idea of how it will look (outside of speculation from seeing Dungeons I and II). And of course, we never got anything magical in Minecraft after Dungeons I.

My point is that IF Mojang were to ever add sorcery themed items or systems, the thematic moment is with the Sift. I might argue it feels as though Mojang has been building towards it since Dungeons but that's a little shaky.
As for how it might appear, I can't say much besides looking at how Minecraft usually introduces systems. Perhaps it will function similarly to all those spell mods, with tomes and staffs.

But it's far more likely that Minecraft will make it unique. Mojang has been quoted saying that they like to add nonconventional/uniquely Minecraft themed things, they actively avoid TROPES and stereotypes.
And I believe the introduction of Souls into Minecraft is their preparation for their uniquely soul themed magic. And, that this update seems the most likely spot for it.

This is just my crackpotting, but what do y'all think?

This subreddit feels completely disconnected from what the Minecraft developers want the game to be.

I have been following Minecraft updates for over a decade, and people have complained that the game feels modded or disappointing after literally every single reveal. But seeing the reaction to this new drop, it is incredibly clear that this subreddit just is not aligned with what the developers want from the game.
For better or worse, a massive chunk of this community wants Minecraft to be more like Terraria or Hytale. They want more progression, more mechanics with heavy consequences, and constant extrinsic motivation and goals to hit.
But Minecraft is not Hytale, and it never will be. There is almost nothing telling you to go kill the Ender Dragon or the Wither. Elytra was added six years after the End, meaning for a lot of the game's lifespan, the only reason you fought the dragon was simply because you wanted to. In fact many people have never killed the Ender Dragon, because that's not what they play Minecraft for.
Minecraft is a sandbox. The best thing you can do in a sandbox is give the player more tools, and that is exactly what this drop does. We are getting a new biome, two block palettes, and a mob with a completely new mechanic. It is a solid drop that leans heavily into the creative, whimsical side of the game. I cannot wait to see what players and myself come up with for this new mob.
People claiming the new slimes have absolutely no use are right in a way. It doesn't have any use for the Minecraft progression. But I don't see why that's a problem. Imagine using piston slimes to knock these things around a base to send redstone signals via pressure plates while they slip and slide everywhere. Imagine if you can put a redstone block in one to activate a line, a netherite block so it does not burn, or a honey block to make it sticky.
Not everything needs a strict progression-based purpose. Having fun, niche uses is a good thing to have in a game. Thats before talking about the obvious use case of them basically adding a ball for any sports game in Minecraft.
It gives me the impression that a lot of people here want Minecraft to become a game its not trying to be.
While the adventure, exploration and combat aspects of this game are important, they aren't the main focus. I don't think they ever will be the main focus. Because as the first trailer for the game put it, Minecraft is a game "Where the only limit is your imagination. Lets go wherever you want to go. How do you want Minecraft to look in 10 years time?

I feel like this is the kind of discussion and feedback that would actually help Mojang get out of the cycle of lots of gimmicky incoherent and half-baked updates that don't really interact with each other. As a community we need to feed them big strategic long-term ideas, not just lots of little fixes or gimmicks here and there.
10 years ago in 2016, we were on version 1.9, the combat update. Think about how much the game has evolved since then. (If you really want to think, the entirety of Minecraft to that point had been built in just 7 years) The game will be very different again in 2036 - or at least, you'd really hope so. So what are the big things you think it should include?
As an example, here are my suggestions - they're deliberately high-level and don't go into every detail, that's the point. They're also still in the theme of vanilla minecraft - ie they're not incongruously modern or inappropriately horrific.

- more options around sharing the game, including the the ability to add mods to realms, or to share worlds between family members without having to have a second device
- new game modes that provide more options for players to choose what kind of game they want to play, including a hybrid creative/survival mode, an ultra-realistic survival mode, and creating workarounds for the problems with peaceful mode

- more biomes, passive, mobs, structures and NPCs in the Nether and (especially) the End, and much more functional (rather than just visual) variety between biomes in the Overworld
-better NPC AI, and more ways to interact and cooperate with villagers, pillagers and traders other than just buying stuff or killing them

- the ability to upgrade workbenches in order to unlock new recipes as you progress through the game. For example, a larger crafting table or brewing stand, and new workbenches that provide new crafting mechanics for the end game. Perhaps some of these workbenches aren't themselves craftable, but only exist in rare structures that you have to seek out to use.
- An expansion of the building process to include building either mobile or instantly breakable structures. So this would allow for people to construct their own tents, boats, wagons, ghast baskets. My idea is that this would require a redstone-enabled assembly platform.

The key point: all these ideas would interact so you get NPCs with their upgraded AI going around on the new mobile structures, and the difference between upgraded biomes is particularly noticeable in ultra-realistic mode. etc etc
Anyway - so what are your BIG ideas for Minecraft 36.1?

text:
Theory: There is a reason the Sift is being added before an End update

Note: all of this is theoretical and unproven, as limited details about the Sift have been revealed

Mojang have said on numerous occasions that a new dimension will not be added until the end is considered complete and it is definitely not complete in its current state. This is common knowledge. So why would they release the Sift while saying this?
Because the Sift will be more endgame than the End. I think that it is incredibly likely, because why would they add a new dimension full of cosmetic content? Mojang is definitely aware that Minecraft is severely lacking in endgame content. Nearly every other part of the game has been addressed through updates and drops, but the only endgame content released in the last eight years were Netherite and the Deep Dark (which is severely underdeveloped too).
Because of the Sift being where the new endgame features would be introduced, they plan to give the End less endgame relevance. I think the End is simply too complex to add endgame features to because of its style. Being empty and barren means that if they add new content, one of two things would happen. One: they spread everything out to keep the empty aesthetic, but players would have to spend far more time exploring an otherwise empty dimension.
Or two: they drop the entire empty and barren aesthetic which would cause other problems (like changing the entire way the End feels as a place).
The reality is that the End was never designed to be anything more than a final boss fight. When Minecraft 1.0 came out, the End had no outer end islands, it was just the dragon fight. Comparing the End to the Nether, the Nether was infinite in its terrain generation, meaning it would be much easier to add new content to. If Mojang wanted the End to be anything more than the boss fight, they would have added the outer end or other end features at launch instead of five years later.
Or at least, they would have designed the End so that it would be easier to add to.
Because of these factors, I think that the reason Mojang has not done an end update yet is because if they did an End update before the Sift was released, players would be disappointed by the lack of new endgame content. The Sift is a completely new concept, which would allow Mojang to fully focus on endgame, instead of trying to fit new stuff into existing content.
They would be better off focusing an entire dimension on endgame stuff, than trying to fit endgame stuff into a dimension that was not meant for it. This means they can have the End specialize in its empty vibe, and the Sift can specialize in its endgame content.
TL;DR: Sift update comes before end update because the content the community would want in an end update would fit better in a new dimension than an existing one.

text:
Is the game too easy, or are the players just good?

I'm sure that by now, most of you will have seen the arguments for the game being too easy, be it that mending is too easy to get, or automated farms kill the survival challenge, or elytra are too overpowered for how easily people can get them, etc.
I want to dispute this idea a little - not by saying that the game is HARD because I absolutely sit in the camp that Minecraft is in no way a difficult game. However, not being difficult is not the same as being "too easy".
The thing I think most people don't consider is that the majority of Minecraft players have been playing for a VERY long time - ranging from a few years to over a decade (I personally have been playing for 12 years now, call me sad all you like). This has inevitably led to a huge amount of skill creep - effectively that the bar for the average player is drastically higher now. People did not have the same ability to minmax every single farm design that they possess now.
People did not have the same ability to blitz through progression that they possess today. You can even take a look at speedrunning as a clear sign of this - the best players in the game 5-6 years ago were beating the game in 20 minutes, while now they've managed to beat the game in just over FIVE.
The point I'm making is that I don't think Minecraft is "too easy", but that people have simply played it for so long that they're accustomed to just about every part of the game. Is it inherently a very forgiving game? Yes, however that can be true and it still is not "too easy".
I'm also not talking about the difficulty of the game for BRAND NEW players, as they may well have an inflated sense of difficulty from everything being new, however I am still challenging the notion that many veterans have that it is TOO easy.

text:
Mojang added the Sift to introduce future bosses to the game.

Fighting a boss became one of the most memorable moments in Minecraft following the addition of the wither and the ender dragon, both of which represents the nether and the end respectively. There is also the elder guardian in the overworld, despite being significantly weaker than the two, and the warden (which I talk more about below).
With each dimension already having a unique boss, I believe one of the problems Mojang has encountered is that they cannot add any more bosses in the game that will feel distinct or coherent to the already existing dimensions.

The overworld should feel neutral, with the exception of hostile mobs that are relatively easy to deal with. The end hosts the ender dragon which I think should remain the last and only boss of the dimension. Adding another boss will  only lower its presence and uniqueness.
Adding a new boss to the nether is an option, but the design must remain true to the hellish atmosphere of the dimension, limiting the space for new and interesting ideas; And I think the Wither already acts as the ultimate boss of the nether similar to the ender dragon.
With the addition of the sift, Mojang now has the excuse to add new bosses to the game. We've seen that the sift is full of souls and (I think) that these souls are able to manifest into distorted versions of life forms, which gives Mojang more space to create interesting boss designs that may otherwise conflict with the design of the other dimensions.
An example is the warden, which is the sole representative of the previously unknown dimension. It is one of the most unique mobs Mojang has added to the game, with it being the only boss to be introduced before its dimension. With its unique design and approach to combat, I am certain that Mojang intended the warden as a teaser on how they are willing to break previously established design conventions for the new mobs that will be added in the game.

text:
Does anyone else feel like Minecraft oceans have become an abandoned concept?

Am I the only one who feels like Minecraft Bedrock is missing genuinely immersive ocean addons?

I’ve noticed that Bedrock, and the minecraft marketplace in particular, have gotten a lot of high-quality addons lately, better world generation, survival mechanics, horror content, structures, etc. But one area that still feels surprisingly underdeveloped is the ocean.
Minecraft’s oceans have so much potential to feel mysterious, atmospheric, and even unsettling, especially in deep water or low visibility situations, but most Bedrock addons barely expand on that aspect at all.
Meanwhile on Java, mods like Thalassophobia show how effective ocean-focused horror and immersion can actually be. It honestly already covers almost everything people seem to want from this type of experience: better atmosphere, deeper and darker oceans, unsettling ambience, more threatening encounters, and an actual fear of exploring deep water.
So as a concrete proposal: why not try to port Thalassophobia to Bedrock? This would be an incredible addition for the marketplace imo, especially for those who prefer to play on console.

Several major Java mods and concepts have already been adapted or recreated for Bedrock in some form, so it feels surprising that nothing similar has happened here yet.

So consider this a semi-serious petition to addon creators:
please give Bedrock players better ocean immersion.
Not necessarily cheap jumpscares or over-the-top monsters, but deeper atmosphere, better ambient audio, more threatening sea life, darker deep oceans, and that feeling of uncertainty when you go too far underwater.

I’m genuinely curious what others think about this.

Do people just not care much about ocean gameplay on Bedrock?
Are there major technical limitations that make something like this difficult to create?
Or has nobody really tried to push the idea yet?
P.S. Alex’s Caves would also be an amazing Bedrock port honestly. And hybrid aquatic tbh would do a brilliant job as well

text:
Seriously hoping The Sift comes with an enchantment overhaul

One of my biggest gripes since the first mob vote was that "The Great Hunger " presented the possibility of a new system that allowed for the addition/removal of enchantments on items. As we all know, Phantoms won and this mechanic hasn't been revisited since.
There's been a big elephant in the room for some years now, which is that 1.14 completely and utterly made the enchanting table obsolete. Before that, enchanting a full set of good equipment was entirely RNG dependant with no way to influence the enchantments you got (past getting the table itself to max level).
With the addition of librarians in 1.14, the process became much more streamlined with the extra bonus that, once you got it fully set up, getting multiple kits of the best gear in the game is simply a matter of having a good way to produce emeralds (which is also villagers).
Everyone (including Mojang) agrees that this is completely busted and breaks progression.
There's even an experimental feature that makes villagers have biome-specific trades and also makes books the last part of a librarian's level up chain among other things; this has been in the game for a couple years but Mojang doesn't dare make it base-game simply because the alternative is reverting to the outdated method of "farm a bajillion XP and then spend hours in front of an enchanting table just rolling die until you get the books/gear you want because Notch was a sadist, or something".
So, my hope is that either The Sift update (or The End Update that is sure to follow) finally addresses the issues with the enchanting table, so the villager trade overhaul can be done without pissing everyone off. Maybe getting items to influence the enchantments we get, or getting a new level up system that allows you to "tune" the enchanting table somehow, with the last level being straight up "yeah okay choose the enchantments, we don't care" (gated behind late endgame content and bosses, of course).
I don't know, anything but whatever the heck the current enchantment table's deal is.

I came up with an idea on how to overhaul the enchanting system to make it more fun

I was playing minecraft and reseting a librarian with a lectern for like 2 hours yesterday and it made me realise just how bad the enchanting system was, so I decided to brainstorm ideas on how Mojang could fix it (and therefore make enchantments like Mending more satisfying to obtain). It still needs some tweaking but here's the overall idea.
It's been clear for years now that the minecraft progression is flawed, especially with systems like enchanting or brewing that never felt rewarding. My idea is to separate all enchantments into 3 different categories (Offensive, Defensive and Misc./Utility), and create 3 different skill trees with each of them. I also thought that separating the enchantment levels to slow down progression could be a good idea although it might make the system too grindy depending on the price of each tree node.
I believe the player should be forced to unlock some of the lesser used enchantments like Smite or BoA (at least in earlier parts of the tree) so that they're forced to engage with them because IMO they are underrated and underutilised. Mostly because it takes the same amount of effort to get sharpness 5 as it takes to get BoA 5 but the actual enchantments aren't equal in power.
The way the player would unlock these enchantments would be by spending a set amount of levels (with some enchantments being more expensive). Important side note - Mojang would need to make levels equal, as you may or may not know, currently leveling up from 0 to 1 takes WAYYYY less XP than from 100 to 101 despite both of these being "one level". The player would then be allowed to put chosen enchantments on the piece of gear they want to enchant.
such action would cost an amount of lapis depending on how many different enchantments the player would choose (a nice way to repurpose lapis within the reworked system). I also thought about the bookshelves, obviously they're so iconic they can't go away.
Bookshelves should be truly optional instead of a requirement, my idea is that each 3 bookshelves around the enchanting table would bring down the lapis price by 7.5% rounded up (I was thinking lapis price should vary between 10 - 90 so a 37.5% decrese in price would feel fair). Additionally it would bring down the level price of unlocking enchantments by (1/2/3) levels on (5/10/15) bookshelves respectively. Finally the books, make them mid to late game loot and take the stronger books away from villagers.
Books should be obtainable from Bastion chests, End city chests, Ancient city chests or as Trial chamber loot etc.
Overall this is what I came up with to fix the unfun nature of traditional minecraft enchanting, as a big terraria fan it makes me sad to see that both sandbox block games have a terrible enchantment system that is neither engaging or fun. Maybe i'll target brewing next if this post gets positive feedback. Feel free to share your opinion and more importantly counter-ideas / constructive criticism. Thank you for attention and see you in the next one. :*

text:
Wish the game had more to it

Minecraft has so many systems that look like they should matter—combat, gear progression, stronger materials, structures, mobs—but none of them actually lead anywhere. Once you beat the Ender Dragon and Wither, there’s no real reason to keep engaging with survival mechanics because nothing pushes back anymore. Building ends up being the only meaningful activity, but even that lacks purpose because your base doesn’t need to defend you from anything.
Why have stronger blocks, traps, or better weapons if there’s no threat that requires them? I’m not asking for some grindy RPG system or constant attacks, just a reason for survival to still feel like survival later in the game. Give building a function, give mobs a purpose beyond early game, and give players something to do that isn’t just building for the sake of it.
I do understand this game is more geared towards building, but in my opinion there are three types of players: builders, redstone players, and fighters. Yet the game only ever really favours builders. Take the Creaking for example—it’s a cool mob with a unique mechanic, but the only real reason to go to that biome is for the wood. A lot of Minecraft just feels like one loop now: new biome, maybe a new mob that doesn’t really do much, and the only reason to go there is for the blocks.
It just feels like the game sets up all these systems—combat, gear, structures—but never actually gives them a proper purpose. I don’t think it needs to turn into some grindy RPG, but it would be nice if survival, combat, and exploration actually mattered as much as building does.

text:
Progression, materials, and keepinventory

I think there’s been a lot of discussion in the community about minecraft’s progression but i think people seem to forget that progression does not have to only be in the form of new materials for all the same tools.

minecraft’s progression is often portrayed as:

get wooden pickaxe -> get 11 cobblestone -> find and smelt iron -> mine diamonds in the first 10 minutes
but this ignores minecraft’s more permanent progression. Materials can be lost upon death, and replacing gear (especially enchanted gear) can take a significant amount of time, but there’s permanent progression that won’t go away as long as you don’t destroy it yourself. completed Nether and End portals, fully booked-up enchantment tables, resource farms. IMO minecraft’s material progression is fine for what it is, it’s these permanent progression markers that are severely lacking.
this also contributes to a growing split of players who play with keepinventory on, because losing your stuff doesn’t really feel like losing progress. Your strip mine is still there, your villager trading hall is still there, there isn’t really anything to ‘rebuild’ or find, it’s just grind and tedium to get back to where you were in terms of gear progression.
IMO the community needs to recognize this permanent progression, enchantment tables and beacons and farms etc., as an extremely valuable means of progress, and i also believe (again, IMO) that minecraft should focus more on this base-building style of progression over the “find this non-renewable resource to get free diamonds or a new type of weapon” progression.
The more minecraft emphasizes the progression of the player’s inventory over the progression of the player’s world, the less fun minecraft is to play as the grind and tedium increase disproportionately to the actual challenge, and the cost of death gets higher and higher.

text:
Toggles that would improve peaceful mode

TLDR at the end, feel free to skip through my ramblings

Many people dislike this but I love peaceful mode. I dont care that I have a "skill issue" or that I play like a baby, sometimes after a long day of real life I dont wanna get attacked by digital monsters while I'm building a block house in my computer.
Anyways, I know other peaceful players have an issue with mob loot: you can't get it. You can't get blaze rods, it's hard to get ender pearls, etc. I think peaceful mode could be greatly improved if hostile mobs still spawned, but became passive (the way the ender dragon does). This way you can kill them and they'll drop their loot, but you're at no risk of harm. The thing is, not everyone would like this change.
Some people don't even want to SEE monsters or have them walking around their builds, which is totally fair. Some people don't like the game changing too much and they want to keep everything the way it is, which is also fair. This is why it should be a setting you can turn on or off when creating a world, the same way you can turn structures generating and TNT explosions on or off.
I also think (and this is much less significant but) you should also be able to turn on hunger in peaceful. Why? Farming gives you something more to do, the game feels kind of empty without EVER needing to grow crops or breed animals. Maybe in peaceful mode they could make it so you cant die of starvation, but they can keep it so you cant run while you need food (just like easy/normal/hard mode).
Again, this should be something you can toggle on or off, because I also understand people finding farming to be a nuisance.
TLDR: hostile mobs still spawning and becoming passive should be something you can optionally turn on in peaceful mode. Hunger should be something you can optionally turn on in peaceful mode. The game should have these as OPTIONS (not a complete change) so everyone can play the way they want.

text:
The Game Drops and The Community expectations

I’ll be honest—I’m getting pretty frustrated with the expectations of the community when it comes to Minecraft game drops. It feels like everything is labeled “bad” or “disappointing” if it isn’t exactly what got hyped up beforehand by influencers or word of mouth.
To me, it almost feels like Mojang only had a few “acceptable” options in the eyes of players: vertical slabs, emerald armor, or an End update—and anything else was doomed to be seen as a letdown.
People also love comparing every new update to older ones, especially the Nether Update, saying things like “updates used to be so much bigger.” But if I’m being honest, I’m still barely in the Nether unless I specifically need something. And I honestly think an End update would face the exact same issue—huge hype, but in practice, most players wouldn’t suddenly spend all their time there.
What also bothers me is this narrative that “Minecraft isn’t putting in effort anymore,” or comments like “finally Minecraft has to try again because Hytale will be so much better.”

The reality is: we’re talking about the best-selling game of all time. Everyone involved has already been massively successful. They don’t have to do anything. Minecraft could have been considered a complete, fully polished game as early as the Village & Pillage update—and it still would’ve stood on its own.
And yet, even today, the game keeps breaking records and bringing in new players every single day.

I think my main point is this: I don’t even know what they could add that would completely blow me away anymore—because I already love the game for what it is. Everything new just feels like a “nice to have,” even if I personally don’t end up using most of it.
Also, the updates themselves aren’t bad. The word I keep seeing is “disappointing”—which is very different. It’s not like something like Pokémon, where recent titles often stand out because of genuinely poor development despite the franchise’s legacy.

At the end of the day, Mojang doesn’t need to reinvent the wheel—and honestly, they probably can’t. But it feels like a lot of people expect exactly that. And it’s kind of sad that everything today has to be bigger, faster, and better to be appreciated.

text:
Minecraft exploration will always be lacklustre, and that’s fine

(Yes the title is bait but I didn’t have a better idea for how to make this point more succinctly)
If you are remotely active on any online space that discusses Minecraft (especially YouTube), you’ve probably heard several complaints about how exploration in Minecraft is not rewarding or satisfying enough to be interesting, and/or how other games do it better. These comments usually range from “the items offered by exploration are not worth it” to “structures are boring and too easy”.
Sometimes proponents of these critiques will blame items like the elytra or quality of life enchantments like mending for “making things too easy” and “incentivising players to stay in one place and not explore”. Many will blame the well known two week Minecraft phase on these issues and claim that if only the game fleshed out these mechanics more, this wouldn’t be as much of a thing.
The reality however, is that Minecraft at its core is just not very replayable as an adventure/exploration game, and this isn’t going to change no matter how much Mojang adds. The game does just not have the level of extrinsic motivation required to sustain the kind of playtime many of its critics want it to provide, such as complex levelling up systems or deep progression.
There is no way to add such features in the breadth many desire without irrevocably changing the character of the game such that it wouldn't really be Minecraft anymore. Any feature that truly changed the game in this direction would compromise the sandbox aspect by gatekeeping content beyond systems that most sandbox-type players will not engage with, actively worsening the experience for them.
Not to mention that sandbox-type players are the ones more likely to actually play the game long-term and avoid the 2 week phase.
As such, smaller "drops" that add to exploration will never be enough to truly satisfy people who want a replayable and detailed exploration game from Minecraft, and won't do anything to stop the 2 week phase.
I think it would honestly be best if Mojang understood this and focused on improving the existing experience with QoL updates or new mechanics that inspire player creativity and intrinsic motivation (like the sulfur cubes) instead of trying to appease people who get bored of new updates within a couple weeks of playing them and quit the game anyway. If you want a game that is focused on extrinsic motivation with mindbogglingly complex progression systems, Minecraft isn't for you, and that's perfectly fine.
Not everything is for everyone, and there are plenty of other great games that cater to players who want a different kind of experience.

text:
Earmuffs for Allays - Keep them as useful companions without them bonding to nearby Note Blocks

The problem:
Allays currently link to any active note block nearby, even when the player doesn't want them to. For example, if you are using an Allay as a companion while gathering wood or mining, simply walking past your base's farms that include note blocks will cause the Allay to link to that note block and abandon you.

The solution: Wool Earmuffs
In Minecraft, wool already dampens sound vibrations (used against Sculk Sensors and the Warden). Allowing players to equip Allays with Wool Earmuffs would be a natural and consistent addition to the game's mechanics.

How It Would Work:

  * Crafting: Crafted simply with 2 Wool and 3 Iron Nuggets for the headband.

  * Equipping: Right-click an Allay to put them on. Sneak + right-click with an empty hand to take them back.
  * Effect: While wearing the earmuffs, the Allay can't hear note block vibrations. It will never link to note blocks and will strictly remain a faithful companion to the player, helping them build tall structures (by bringing back fallen blocks) and gather resources.

  * Visuals & Customization: They show up as tiny, adorable earmuffs on the Allay's head and can be crafted in all 16 wool colors!
I've also submitted this to the official Minecraft Feedback site if you'd like to support the idea there: https://feedback.minecraft.net/hc/en-us/community/posts/48978540335501-Earmuffs-for-Allays

The in-game visuals were custom-made by me using Blockbench and rendered in-game to show how this feature could look.
